summary:
ZYNTARA: Flame in Freefall
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 | Team ZYNTARA (solo: Azhan Ahmed Siddiqui)

Fire behaves very differently in microgravity. Without buoyancy, flames turn spherical and burn in ways Earth-based intuition cannot predict, which makes spacecraft fire safety a hard problem. NASA has run many combustion experiments in space (BASS, FLEX, SAME/SAME-R, SAFFIRE, CFI), but the results are spread across separate investigations and tables, so they are slow to compare.

ZYNTARA is a web-based research workspace that brings this data together and makes it explorable. A FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend ingests real NASA investigation data while preserving the provenance of every record. Pandas, NumPy and SciPy handle the analysis. A scikit-learn model ranks the factors that matter, and SHAP explains why each result was ranked the way it was. An optional LLM only turns those results into readable text and never computes the ranking itself. A React and TypeScript frontend, with Three.js and Recharts, presents everything in an interactive dashboard.

ZYNTARA follows a strict rule: no fabricated data, no arbitrary safety thresholds, and simulations are always labeled. This keeps every insight traceable to real NASA data.

Live demo: https://zyntara-frontend.vercel.app/
GitHub: https://github.com/azhanahmed22-beep/NS-FLAME-IN-FREE-FALL
details:
Project name: ZYNTARA: Flame in Freefall
Challenge: Flame in Freefall (NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026)
Team: ZYNTARA (solo participant: Azhan Ahmed Siddiqui)

What it does

ZYNTARA is a research workspace for microgravity combustion science. It brings together data from NASA fire experiments, analyzes it, ranks the factors that matter, and explains the results through an interactive web dashboard.

Problem it addresses

In microgravity, flames do not rise and behave differently than on Earth, so spacecraft fire safety cannot rely on Earth-based assumptions. NASA experiment data is spread across many investigations and file formats, which makes it slow to compare materials, fuels and test conditions.

Data used

Real NASA investigation data, cleaned and summarized with the source file name kept for provenance:

Dataset

What it contains

PSI-101 Experimental Table (SAME-R)

109 test records across 5 materials (Kapton, Silicone, Lampwick, Pyrell, Teflon): inlet velocity, heating ratio, duration, aging and mixing times

SAME-R Detection by Test

45 tests: obscuration, scattering and ionization signals for smoke detection

SAME-R Detection by Material

5 materials summarized: for example Silicone shows the strongest smoke signal, while Kapton and Teflon show almost none

PSI-115 Summary

44 rows comparing Earth gravity vs microgravity (8 cm and 10 cm cases) across 17 variables such as smoke, number density, temperature and velocity

PSI-117 Extinction

93 rows for n-dodecane, n-decane and n-heptane at 0.5 to 5.0 atm, labeled experiment (54) or model (39)

Priority NASA investigations: BASS and BASS-II, FLEX and FLEX-2, SAME and SAME-R, SAFFIRE I, II, III, and CFI.

How the AI works

  1. Ingestion: data is loaded with its source and provenance preserved.
  2. Analysis: Pandas, NumPy and SciPy handle cleaning and statistics.
  3. ML ranking: scikit-learn ranks the factors that matter.
  4. Explainability: SHAP shows why each result was ranked the way it was.
  5. AI interpretation (optional): an LLM turns the results into readable summaries. It never computes the ranking.

Technology stack

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Alembic, Pydantic v2, JWT authentication, Pytest, Docker Compose
  • Data and ML: Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, SHAP
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js / React Three Fiber, Framer Motion, Recharts, Axios
  • Deployment: Vercel (frontend and API), GitHub

Design principles

  • Never fabricate NASA data, citations or URLs
  • Preserve provenance for every record
  • No arbitrary safety thresholds
  • Simulations are clearly labeled
